pointers.sentence: `reverse` and the `{% url %}` tag already turned names into paths in Django 1.1 (`docs/releases/1.1.txt`), when every pattern was a regular expression.
Routes, and `path` to write them, came in 2.0 as a "simplified URL routing syntax", and the function that had written patterns until then was made available as `re_path` (`docs/releases/2.0.txt`).

Routes were fitted to the machinery already there (`deps:final/0201-simplified-routing-syntax.rst`): a route is expanded into a regular expression as its matcher is made (`django/urls/resolvers.py:_route_to_regex`), and reversing works on expressions whichever function wrote the pattern.

Routes were fitted to the machinery already there (`deps:final/0201-simplified-routing-syntax.rst`): a route is expanded into a regular expression as its matcher is made (`django/urls/resolvers.py:_route_to_regex`), and reversing works on expressions whichever function wrote the pattern.

`reverse` itself finds the root resolver of the current URLconf, unless it is given a URLconf, reads the script prefix, deals with any namespaces in the name, and hands the rest to `URLResolver._reverse_with_prefix`: the name, the prefix, and the arguments, which are given either as a list or as a dictionary (`django/urls/base.py:reverse`).

It runs when something needs the tables and finds none for the language in use, and it runs again, on a resolver lower down, each time a resolver above it is populated (`django/urls/resolvers.py:URLResolver._populate`).

Each of its candidates is filed again in the upper table under the same key, with the include's regular expression put in front of its own, its forms made afresh from the longer expression, and the include's extra arguments and converters merged with its own; where both give an extra argument of the same name, the include's is kept here (`django/urls/resolvers.py:URLResolver._populate`), though the view is called with the pattern's ([Resolving a path](resolving.md#how-the-arguments-are-merged)).

Django's documentation relies on that order: a project that wants its own view at a name an application already uses, a login page for one, is told to write its pattern after the application's include (`docs/topics/http/urls.txt`).

The pass also fills a set on the side, `URLResolver._callback_strs`, with the dotted name of every view in the tree, namespaced or not, from which `URLResolver._is_callback` answers whether a dotted name is that of a view of the URLconf; the admin's documentation asks it before it imports a view named in its address (`django/contrib/admindocs/views.py:ViewDetailView._get_view_func`).
Then it tries each form of each candidate, in order, against the arguments (`django/urls/resolvers.py:URLResolver._reverse_with_prefix`).
The documentation allows an extra argument to have the name of a parameter its route captures, and the extra argument then replaces the capture (`docs/topics/http/urls.txt`).

`reverse` neither requires such a parameter nor holds it to the extra argument's value: a call that gives it fits with any value, and a call by keyword that leaves it out fits too, since the extra arguments' names are not compared, but then nothing fills its gap, and `reverse` raises `KeyError`, not `NoReverseMatch` (`django/urls/resolvers.py:URLResolver._reverse_with_prefix`).
And a result that begins with two slashes has the second replaced by `%2F`, so that a browser cannot read the path as the name of another host (`django/utils/http.py:escape_leading_slashes`).

The check is made on the unescaped text because that is what the resolver is matched against: "WSGI provides decoded URLs, without %xx escapes, and the URL resolver operates on such URLs," says the comment above it (`django/urls/resolvers.py:URLResolver._reverse_with_prefix`).

Such code may be imported by the URLconf itself, and a plain `reverse` there asks for patterns that do not yet exist ([When a URLconf is imported](import.md#when-the-import-fails)) (`django/urls/base.py:reverse_lazy`, `django/utils/functional.py:lazy`).
